prompt:
Discuss the solvability of the system of equations
$$\begin{aligned}\lambda x + y + z &= a\\ x + \lambda y + z &= b\\ x + y + \lambda z &= c\end{aligned}$$
for all numbers $\lambda, a, b, c \in \mathbb R$.
answer: For $\lambda\notin\{1,-2\}$ there is exactly one solution, $x=\frac{(\lambda+1)a-b-c}{(\lambda-1)(\lambda+2)}$ (and cyclically); for $\lambda=1$ it is solvable iff $a=b=c$ (two-parameter family); for $\lambda=-2$ it is solvable iff $a+b+c=0$ (one-parameter family). The determinant is $(\lambda-1)^2(\lambda+2)$.

solutions.title: Determinant and case analysis
solutions.body:
The coefficient matrix is $A=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&1&1\\1&\lambda&1\\1&1&\lambda\end{pmatrix}=(\lambda-1)I+J$, where $J$ is the all-ones matrix. $J$ has eigenvalues $3,0,0$, so $A$ has eigenvalues $\lambda+2,\lambda-1,\lambda-1$ and
$$\det A=(\lambda-1)^2(\lambda+2).$$

**Case $\lambda\ne1,\ \lambda\ne-2$.** Then $\det A\ne0$ and the system has exactly one solution for every $a,b,c$. Explicitly: adding the three equations gives $(\lambda+2)(x+y+z)=a+b+c$, so $S:=x+y+z=\frac{a+b+c}{\lambda+2}$. The first equation reads $(\lambda-1)x+S=a$, hence
$$x=\frac{a-S}{\lambda-1}=\frac{(\lambda+1)a-b-c}{(\lambda-1)(\lambda+2)},$$
and similarly $y=\frac{(\lambda+1)b-a-c}{(\lambda-1)(\lambda+2)}$, $z=\frac{(\lambda+1)c-a-b}{(\lambda-1)(\lambda+2)}$.

**Case $\lambda=1$.** All three equations have left side $x+y+z$. So the system is solvable iff $a=b=c$, and then the solutions are $x=a-u-v,\ y=u,\ z=v$ with $u,v\in\mathbb R$ arbitrary (infinitely many, a plane of solutions). If $a,b,c$ are not all equal there is no solution.

**Case $\lambda=-2$.** Adding the equations gives $0=a+b+c$, so $a+b+c=0$ is necessary. Conversely, if $a+b+c=0$, the third equation is minus the sum of the first two, so it is redundant. The matrix has rank $2$ (the first two rows are independent), so there is a one-parameter family of solutions. Subtracting the second equation from the first gives $-3x+3y=a-b$. So with $x=t$:
$$x=t,\qquad y=t+\frac{a-b}{3},\qquad z=t+\frac{2a+b}{3}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
(Check: $x+y-2z=\frac{a-b-4a-2b}{3}=-a-b=c$.) If $a+b+c\ne0$ there is no solution.

**Summary.** Unique solution for $\lambda\notin\{1,-2\}$; for $\lambda=1$ infinitely many solutions if $a=b=c$ and none otherwise; for $\lambda=-2$ infinitely many solutions if $a+b+c=0$ and none otherwise. ∎

prompt: Let $f(x)$ be an even twice differentiable function such that $f''(0)\neq 0$. Prove that $f(x)$ has a local extremum at $x=0$.
answer: Evenness forces $f'(0)=0$ (the one-sided difference quotients are negatives of each other); then $f''(0)\ne0$ and the second-derivative test give a strict local extremum.

solutions.title: Show $f'(0)=0$, then the second-derivative test
solutions.body:
**Step 1: $f'(0)=0$.** Since $f$ is differentiable at $0$,
$$f'(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}.$$
Replacing $h$ by $-h$ and using $f(-h)=f(h)$,
$$f'(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(-h)-f(0)}{-h}=-\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=-f'(0),$$
so $f'(0)=0$. (Equivalently: differentiating $f(-x)=f(x)$ gives $-f'(-x)=f'(x)$, and $x=0$ gives $f'(0)=0$.)

**Step 2: second-derivative test.** Suppose $f''(0)>0$ (the case $f''(0)<0$ is the same with $-f$). Because $f'(0)=0$,
$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f'(x)}{x}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f'(x)-f'(0)}{x}=f''(0)>0 .$$
Hence there is $\delta>0$ with $f'(x)/x>0$ for $0<|x|<\delta$, i.e. $f'(x)>0$ on $(0,\delta)$ and $f'(x)<0$ on $(-\delta,0)$. For $0<x<\delta$ the mean value theorem gives $f(x)-f(0)=f'(\xi)x$ with $\xi\in(0,x)$, so $f(x)>f(0)$; for $-\delta<x<0$ similarly $f(x)-f(0)=f'(\xi)x$ with $\xi\in(x,0)$, a product of two negative numbers, so again $f(x)>f(0)$.

Thus $f$ has a strict local minimum at $0$ if $f''(0)>0$ and a strict local maximum if $f''(0)<0$. ∎

prompt: Let $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ be mutually inverse decreasing functions on the interval $(0,\infty)$. Can it hold that $f(x)>g(x)$ for all $x\in(0,\infty)$?

solutions.title: The official example
solutions.body:
The official answer is **yes**. Take
$$f(x)=-\tfrac12x-1,\qquad g(x)=-2x-2 .$$
Both are decreasing (negative slopes), and they are mutually inverse: $g(f(x))=-2\left(-\tfrac12x-1\right)-2=x$ and $f(g(x))=-\tfrac12(-2x-2)-1=x$ for all $x$. For $x>0$,
$$f(x)-g(x)=\tfrac32x+1>0,$$
so $f(x)>g(x)$ on the whole interval $(0,\infty)$.

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

solutions.title: Remark: what if both functions map $(0,\infty)$ onto itself?
solutions.body:
In the example the values of $f$ and $g$ on $(0,\infty)$ are negative, so the inverse relation uses $g$ outside $(0,\infty)$. It helps to see why that cannot be avoided.

Suppose $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is a decreasing bijection with inverse $g:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$. A monotone bijection between intervals is continuous. Also $f(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ and $f(x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$ (the range is all of $(0,\infty)$). So $h(x)=f(x)-x$ is continuous, tends to $+\infty$ at $0^+$ and to $-\infty$ at $\infty$, and has a zero $x_0$. Then $f(x_0)=x_0$, hence $g(x_0)=x_0=f(x_0)$, and the strict inequality fails at $x_0$.

So the answer *yes* depends on reading the statement as in the official solution: $f$ and $g$ are inverse to each other as functions on $\mathbb R$ and decreasing, and the inequality is only required for $x\in(0,\infty)$.
